From the St. Thomas Times , A'oue nlier 5, 1845 We insert below a translation o a proclamation issued bv the Haytien Government, and published ttt the Manifeste. 1 be number containing it, which has reached us is dated the 11th ult., but the document was signed bv President Pierrot on the 30th Sept. It will be seen by perusing it, that ail foreign vessels trading with the Eastern portion of the island, are liable to he seized and sold for the ben fit of the State, and those or board to be treated as (eontrabandistes) smugglers. But will the maritime powers acknowledge the legality of this decree? which is neither a blockade de jure, nor de facto. The ports are simply declared closed to foreign commerce , and unless a sufficient force he kept on the coast to enforce the regulation it will be absolutely worthless, and even in that case we cannot conceive how it can be allowed. In the first place the Haytiens are not in possession of the ports in the Eastern part, and to close them according to the law of nations, an actual and efficient blockade must he established, due notice given to foreigners, and its legality acknowledged by the dominant powers þÿ How can vessels now trading to Eastern ports he declared and treated as smugglers when they visit the ports openly, and enter their cargoes in the custom houses established bv the authorities in possession. It is true that for -J of a century the Spanish quarter has been an integral portion of ilia Republic of þÿllavti but they have declared their Independence and it yet remains

to be seen whether the Haytien government will be aide to reduce them to submission. In the menu tin e, we do not thit k that foreign powers will permit the vessels sailing under the protection of their Hags to fie seized and confiscated if they are þÿ taken in the act of prosecuting a pc-acetul commetce, and are not detected in carrying munitions ot war or in committing other acts which would þÿpie elude them from claiming the protection of their þÿHag such as transporting Hoops, material die.

The American papers just received furnish the following particulars of the near completion of the north-eastern boundary survey: þÿ "Three parties commenced operations about i he 1st of MaV þÿ one under the charge of I. lent. Emery of the Topographical Hu- -eao, who surveyed the line from the third of the Connecticut lakes to the head of the Dead River, the point where the survey closed last vcar. The second party was under the charge of Lieut. Warner, also of the Topographical Bureau, whose duty it was to survev the route from Canaan west. The third party was under the charge of Mr. Longfellow of Portland, who surveyed the route Irom the head of Hall Stream (where the boundsrv defined by the treaty he.gins to take the highlands), to the third Connecticut lake. The first of these parties dosed their work on the 3d instant, and the olher two will close their field service ii« a few days. The three parties numbered, all told, between 200 and 300 persons , many of them being attached to the commissary departments, and some of whom are known as þÿ suckers, or packmen1 The service of these men is particularly arduous, their duly being to bring the provisions upon their ktaclis over a country that is not passable except for men. a st ronomicn I ohser va t ions. The work of the surveying parties has been concluded two months eailier than was anticipated. DISASTROUS NEWS FROM ALGERIA. The Algiers journals of the 1st give an account of an affair which has just taken place near I )j ma Ghaxout. An officer who commanded that post being informed by a subjected Arab Chief that Abdel Kader, at tiie head of only a lew men, had come to seek a refuge in the environs, and was then in a spot where he might he easily surprised, set out with a small column of 450 mew. On arriving at the marabout ol'Sidi Brah'ra (lour leagues Irom Djema Giiazout), he was suddenly surrounded by an enormous mass of horsemen and Ivahyles of the country. The melee vs as terrible, (or in a moment officers and soldiers were stretched lifeless on the earth, with the exception of 80 men of the Chasseurs, at the head of whom was Captain Goreaux. the only officer who had n.d been killed. Notwithstanding the efforts of the enemy, these 80 men got possession of a neighbouring marabout, and shut themselves up in it. Three times did Abdel Kader call upon them to surrender, swearing that no harm should b« dwne to them, for, said he, you are humane towards Mussulman prisoners." Although reduced to the last extiemily the brave men would not listen to any terms, and under these circumstances Abdel ivadcr retired, leaving a large force to blockade the marabout. Scarcely was the hulk of llie besieging force out of sight of the besieged, than they attempted a sortie, and penetrating the line of natives who surrounded them, directed their course towaids Djema Gliazoural. At a league Irom that place a
host of Ivahyles fell uporn them, and 12 only out of the number escaped.

A Romance of Real þÿLife. One of my father's brothers, residing in Boston at that time, became a victim to the pestilence (the yellow fever ftien prevailing). When the lirst svmptoms appeared, his wife sent the cliildien into the countiy and herself remained to attend upon him. Her friends warned her against such rashness '1 hey told tier it would lie deatfi to tier, and no benefit to him, for lie would soon be too ill to know who attended upon him. She accordingly stayed ami watchad liini with utiteiiuiiing cure. '1 his, however, did not avail to save him. He grew worse and worse, and finally died. 1 hose who went round with the death carts had visited the chamber, and seen that I tie end was near. They now came to take the body. His wife refused to let it go. She told me she never knew how to account for it, but though he was perfectly cold and ligid, and to everv appearance quite dear), there was a powerful impression on her mind that life was not extinct. The men were ovetborne by the strength of her conviction, though their own reason was opposed to it. The hall hour again came round, and again was heard the solemn wotds, " Bring out the dead.'' The wile again lesisted their importunities; but this time the men w ere more resolute, Thev said the duty assigned to them was a painful one ; but the health of

the city inquired punctual obedience to the orders they received: if they ever expected the pestilence to abate, it must be bv a prompt removal of the dead, and immediate fumigation of the infected apartments. She pleaded and pleaded, and even knell to them in an agony of tears, continually saying, "1 am sine he is not dead." To all their remonstrances she answered. " If you bury him, you shall bury me with him.'1 At last, by dint of reasoning on the necessity of the case, they obtained from her a promise that it he showed no signs of life before they again came round, she would make no further opposition to the removal. The Minerals of Aloiers. þÿ The Commerce (French paper), in an article on the mineral resources of Algiers, gives the following statements; þÿ The principal veins discovered in Algeria are of copper, iron and lead. 7'hose of copper arid iron may give good results if they are worked with intelligence. As to the lead, however abundant it may be, it appears to be situated in positions little accessible to industry, and could not probably sustain a competition with the rich tninss of Spain, and the United States of America, The copper mine of the Teniah ot Monzzin, is the only one for which there has been as yet a government concession, but the wonders related of it have led to numerous demands for other grants. It appears, however, that the yield is by no means so rich as lias heen staled. The ore is in a very mixed state, and only a small portion of it gives 25 per cent.; whereas it had been reported that this was the produce of the entire mass, and in order to obtain the 25 per cent, from the richest portion of the ore it has to undergo a very tedious and expensive process, and has to be carried at a great expense to Blidali, and from thence to Al giers. As the average yield of the ore is only 10 to 12 per cent., the speculation cannot be a very lucrative one, when the expense of carriage to \lgiers, and of transport to Marseilles, is taken into account. There are other veins of copper in the environs of Tenet, close to the sea. but the works that have ben undertaken in order to ascertain
their value, are not yet sufficiently advanced tor any just notion to be formed on the sub-

ST, ATI3, ject. Algeria is richer in iron than copper. In the environs of Blidnh there is a compact iron ore, and on the crown of the Atlas be tween Biidah and Medeah, there are iron and copper to great extent. This is also the case in many ether parts of Algeria, and speculators are not more anxious to obtain grants for iron mines than tor those of copper ; but, as the Commerce observes, it is not suflicieut to have iron ore, but to know how to convert it into iron with speed and economy The conclusion o! the Commerce is, that Algeria does not present, as regards mines, such resources for smelling, carriage, die, as to justify the vast ideas thai have been conceived ol it.

In the midst of mirth and gaiety, of dance and song, and jocund laughter þÿ the words of the inspired Psalmist þÿ " in the midst of life we are in death" were awfully exemplified þÿ a fellow-being was hurried into eternity þÿ His sent to his great reckoning unprepared, and by the hand of one of his acquaintances. The name of the unfortunate victim was Santiago, and that of his murderer Joseph Ross. As the horrid deed was committed the guilty wretch fled þÿ hut he was caught tins morning in the country, brought into town and is now incarcerated in the fort þÿ there to await the doom which offended Jus tiee may decree. May a sincere repentance occupy his heart till summoned before the eternal judge to answer for his misdeeds. On the morning of the New Year, two lads, one, much the senior of the other, were quarelling together þÿ half in jest and earnest, when the younger in a fit of passion stabbed the elder with a penknife, wounding him seriously. The sufferer was conveyed to the hospital, where he now lies we belirve in a dangerous state.

CITY NEWS. Concerts þÿ <)ie Bull took his leave as an artist last evening, and both he and the public will remember the occasion with interest. The Tabernacle w-as filled to the utmost, Erotn six till eight the crowd was gathering and condensing till it became one compact mass, and all the available seats, and even the aisles down to the stage, were occupied. In one of the galleries near the stage sat the pupils of the Institution for lite Blind, who were there by invitation, and their peculiar delight in the music added to the general interest <>t the evening. We never heard the great professor snr. pass the effect l»! produced last evening. His genius seemed to take new warmth from his heart, and Ins exquisite harmonies were expressions of most refined feeling. Doubtless the consciousness that he was speaking for the last time to many, between whom and himself a warm sympathy has grown up, gave an additional earnestness to his tones, and increased softness to the measure ot his pieces. The concerto in E minor, containing a beautiful adagio movement, descriptive of exter tial natuie, was a brilliant performance though somewhat injured by want of preparation in the orchestra. Rut his Niagara was poured forth with great power and beauty, and the mingled tenderness of the spectator's reverie with the grandeur of the scene, was a untile triumph of art. Me afterwards appealed in a duett with Miss Northall, and showed the wonderful power of his violin in rivalling the sottest

tones of the human voice. The Cartnival of Venice was received, as it always has been, with raptures, and after it ceased the applause was so loud and continued that lie returned and gave a new piece without accompaniment. This was one of the most touching expressions of feeling ever heard in this city. It was between the performer and his own heart, and to the listener it was a most lender memory of the past in his own experience.

' Alemorv of Washington" closed the > c evening, and never did a successful career end with a more brilliant tribute by geimrs to greatness. 1'iie march was given with great eflect, and the stately measure of the whole, the pure and upright spirit which breathes through it, attested the author's appreciation of his great subject. When it ceased amid the uproar of applause, bouquets and wreaths tell upon tire stage in prolusion. J lie leaner of the orchestra attempted to ciown film, but he resisted and came loiw.ud to the auuiciice, homing a laurel wieaih in tils hand Pale and evidently agitated by the occasion, lie said þÿ ' Ladies and Gentle men this wreath must wittier þÿ þÿ its leaves must þÿdie but the memory of tins hour will never die in this guileful heart." Up to the hour of going to press this (lay, it is a matter of doubt whether Lord John Russell will take upon himself the task of forming a new ministry. The Morning Chronicle of this morning thus expresses itsell upon the point: þÿ -'Lord John Russell has not yet undertaken the task ot forming an Administration ; and it is not unlikely that two or three days may elapse before the noble lord Can be in possession of the information which would warrant him in taking that important step. Upon this point we can only say what we have said before, that the Liberal leader would not be doing justice to the great principle with the maintenance of which he is identified, nor to t he party with which he is connected, nor to himself, in accepting the responsibilities of government at the present crisis, without a clear prospect «J being able to ejfecl an abolition of the cornlaws." This clear prospect, it appears, mainly depends upon the lull and frank co operation of Sir R. jpVont þÿJfe/Z i Weakly Messenger, London December 8, 1845. LATEST NEWS FROM PORTUGAL. Bv the Black Eagle, steam packet from Lisbon, advices have been received from Portugal to the 29th ult. The only intelligence of importance is contained in the fol lowing extract from the letter of the private correspondent ot the Herald ; þÿ The Portuguese Ministers are at present busy in the concoction of one of the most extraordinary, and it may be added arbitrary financial measures ever conceived. 1'or the belter understanding of the meditated measure a few prefatory explanations are necessary. lu Portugal there are no church-rates. The parochial clergy are supported partly by voluntary contributions from a portion of the parishioners, who form themselves into a Cnnjraria, or confraternity, for that express purpose, and partly from the revenues derived from houses, lands, and other property, acquired in limes past by gift or bequest, rev- or purchased with the accumulated surplus this enues of former years. The whole of property is in the hands of the confraternities, who pay the parochial clergy their stipends, but manage all the concerns of the churches þÿthemselves a system which has always worked admirably well as it has provided l<>r tne decent and comfortable subsistence ot the priests, and at the same time saved them from the odium of being or even appearing burdensome to those under their spiritual care. Besides the parochial confraternities, property of the same kind and acquired in the same manner is held, to a very large extent, bv many other corporate bodies

throughout the whole country, such as the nunneries, the municipalities, and the various hospitals and other charitable establishments. Tiie measuie to which 1 aliude is to the effect that all the confraternities, nunneries, municipalities, and charitable institutions shall be obliged to sell the whole of the property they hold, and invest the proceeds in Government Inscriptions. The government is to compel all persons holding money at interest from anv of those corporations to pay up every' farthing of the principal, the amount of which is in like manner to be invested in Inscriptions ; and further, although the immemorial law ot Portugal forbids the alteration of an entail, except with the consent of the next heir to it, the actual possessor is to fie allowed to sell his property without the concurrence of his heir, provided he invests the proceeds in Inset iptions, to he deposited in the cusmdy of the Board of Public Credit, as an equally inalienable entailed property. This sweeping measure, by withdrawing an immense amount of Inscriptions from the market would no doubt greatly raise their value, perhaps even bring them up to par ; but, however well fitted it may he to produce the desired effect, there is no question that it would be a most flagrant violation ot the rights of property. An intimation has been made by the gov. eminent to the directors of the Union Company, to the effect that they must either break up their savings banks within 30 days, or invest a moiety of the money deposited in

them in Inscriptions. flow the directors mean to act in this perplexing dilemma remains to be seen. They have, hotvever, called upon the shareholders for a further instalment of 20 milrcis per share, which

s tr 12- m $> n £ T& & looks very much as if they intended to pay back all their deposits rather than submit to the condition imposed upon them. A Royal decree, dated the 15th, and published in tire Diario of the 22d instant, ordains the raising of 8000 -recruits, in order, as it is therein stated, to bring the effective force of the army up to 24,000 men, in accordance with the regulation of the 9th July, 1842, which fixed it at that number. The cargo of the British barque Lee, recently stranded near Faro, on the coast of Algarve, lias been landed. It consists of about 1200 packages, the greater part of which have escaped damage.

It was contained in a letter to him, from a friend, in the north of England, 'i he parties referred to are all personal friends of his family þÿ þÿ Trade here is in an awfully stagnated state; and we are expecting such a crash as has seldom or never been known in L . You will, before this, have tieard of poor if þÿ suicide. The family have wisely kept all as secret as possible but speculation has left his widow and child dependent on their friends for everything. 1 1 is widow will be confined of her second child in the ensuing mouth. A has stopped payment; he has lost in speculation 12,000/ þÿ He is able to oiler 6s, 8d. in the pound, which will be accepted. F. poisoned himself this morning, solely from the consequences of injudicious share jobbing. He leaves a large family with sorry prospects. Twenty years of unsullied reputation have thus been blasted bv six months of tolly. P. and Co. have shut up; and they have told me themselves that they have not one penny left !Six months ago, H came into the house with a capital of 5000/., and it is all gone. VYc have many more miner cases ot suffering ; and, perhaps, no family in this district can say, that individually and relatively they are unscathed by tins devastating þÿmania. þÿ lidfast Whig, MckiIeii Prevented by Teetotai.ism. þÿ We find the following in a late number ot the

Liverpool Mercury: þÿ þÿ On Wednesday evening, at the total abstinence meeting in Bevington Hill, p.u individual came in considerably the worse for liquor, whilst a Mr. Strick, front Leeds, was, speaking and pointing out the awful consequences that had occurred in his own family through the love of strong drink. It wrought so much upon the mind and conscience of the individual alluded to, that he came forward and produced a pistol, which he had purchased that evening for the purpose of shooting his wife, said he felt conscious of the evil of drink, and signed the pledge.

Gamblers Abroad. þÿ A letter from Ham1 burg, of Nov. 21, in the Frankfort Journal, says, þÿ flow many gamblers have sacrificed ilieir fortune in the hope of inventing a system to gain infallible at play, and not one has succeeded ! What I am going to relate is singular, but it is irue, and causes a great sensation þÿhere Within the last few days there has arrived from Brussels a company, having at its head Baron de V., which purposes opening a regular attack on the gaminghouses. It has its cashier, controller, &c.,

possesses a capital of 260,000 florins (1040 shares at 250 florins each), and asserts that having tried the system at Brussels for a period of four months, it is certain that if it had played against a public establishment, it should have gained 3,000.000 florins, without losing a single day. From the St Thamus Tunes, 14 th Jan. 1 H4 1j From our London Correspondent. þÿDecb r, It!, 1815. Since the departure of the last packet the events that have occurred, have been ot the most extraordinary and astounding character. And as yet there is -no clearing up of the surprises and uncertainties that have shaken the country to its centre. To under stand the causes of this extraordinary excitement, it will be necessary to detail the events of the last few days, the result of which has been that the conservative ministry has of its accord resigned, and Lord John Russell has been summoned to the councils oi the Queen. Your readers will have no doubt attentively perused Lord John Russell's letter of 2 2d November, to his constituents of the city of London. The noble Lord had therein expressed his surprise that, after so many meetings of the Cabinet, no result had apparently been come to by ministers, to make provision for the deficiency ol the wheat harvest in England, and the scarcity ot food, in consequence ol the failure of the potato crop in Ireland. The noble Lord declared himself decidedlv in favour of an Entire Repeal of " Corn and Provision þÿlaws,, renouncing all his former claims either for fixed duly, or of any modification thereof ; and as the þÿ(Queen s ministers did not announce their decision, he called on us þÿ the Queen 's þÿsubjects- to come forward and demand an entire and unconditional repeal. It is a curious instance of tmw minds are influenced, and jump together, for the same paper that contained this letter,

dated Edinburgh 22d November, also contained a letter ol a similar spirit from Lord Morpeth at Leeds, handing £5 to the funds of the League, thereby pledging himself to the principles of that body. Mean'inie meetings were being held by corporate and other bodies over the country, and uieuioiials were ponied in to the Prime Ministers from all parts, and from every description ot politicians, imploring even a temporal v relaxation ot the sliding scale. The Whig leaders were everv where m trout renouncing their old opinions, and unreservedly joining with the League orators in demanding an immediate and unconditional abolition ol me corn laws. The press of London was lead on in this emergency by the Times, day alter day its leaders denounced the hesitation of ministers. It pointed to t ie Duke ot Wellington as the þÿ Lion in Hie þÿpath, and called on the Premier to resign if he could not bring his colleagues to agree to that measure, that could alone save this country from extreme scarcity and Ireland from immediate famine. In the meantime it was well known that the corn in bond in the stores in this country, was being exported to Holland and Belgium, and that the corn commissioners who were appointed to enquire into the failure of the potato crop in Ireland, were completely at fault, and that there appeared no prospect of cheeking the ravages of this unseen and unknown enemy, or o! saving even one half of the crop from destruction. Such was the state of atiairs when surprise was added to embar-

rassment, by the announcement of the Times of the 4th December, that þÿ the decision of the Cabinet was no longer a þÿsecret, Parliament was to be called together the first week in January ; the Royal Speech to command

6T V $ 0 1 21 A T '1 3 an immediate consideration of the corn laws preparatory to their total repeal, and Sir Robert Peel in one house, and the Duke oi Wellington in the other were prepared to give immediate effect to the recommendations thus conveyed. To this announcement the professedly ministerial papers at first gave a hesitating denial, but the Times persisted in the coriectness of its information, and ultimately, events proved the uuth ol its assertions.

The amazement this announcement caused can be but inadequately described. That he! who had been selected by the Landlord and farming interests, and placed in power by them to defend and protect those inteiests, snould have turned round, and not only eon sented hut obtained the eoncui renoe of Ins colleagues to tins sweeping meausure surpass ed the understanding ot the agricultural mind. The meicantile public were in raptures The Leadeis ot l tie l.eague alone were cautious, iiui ihe announcement was enough lo Ian the flames of agitation to its greatest hi int, and meetings and memorials wete redout) ed fioin Johnny Gloat's House lo the Laud's End. The End however is not yet, u litile war hud but passed; cabinet meetings were still being held, abd only the repeated declarations of the Tunes, þÿ denied by other papers were to satislv ihe public in the uncertainty. The miiustiy made no sign, time cabinet meetings had been held and dispersed, and still the public was in doubt and perplexity. W hen at length the ministei s went in a body and tendered their resignations to Her Majesty at Osborne House. On Sunday the ministry resigned. The Queen uskt.d Siir Robert Peel whom lie recommended tier to send for. lie begged lo decline advising. Her Majesty then said she would send for Lord John Russell, and Sir Robert observed that her Majesty would do quite light. Lord John Russell, laid attended the þÿQueen summons s and subsequently bail several audiences of her Majesty. He lias also

met several ol his formci colleagues but as yet no ministry lias been funned. In fact the circumstances have neeu enough to warrant exlieme caution ni any statesman laking office at such a time, and on such u subject. The landlords aie indignant ai the þÿ Dodge1' about to be played oti them by their own mini on, and it was Hie withdrawal ol ihcir proxies, which they bad placed in tbe hands ol llie Duke ot Wellington, and the dread ot their opposition that induced the Iron Duke to withdraw his support to a measure lo which he na i given but a reluctant consent, and which caused the breaking up ol the strongest ministry that ever field the reigns of power. Under these circumstances the l ieu traders alone are rejoiced they are holding meetings of congratulation and yet of cautious advice all over the country, they advise no huzzaing, until Hie abrogation of the Corn Laws be on the Stutute Book. They entreat and implore of their friends to obtain Freehold votes, so as to win counties, and they are buckling on their armour vv th the lived determination to elleot their object fully and entirely. A meeting m Manchester last week indicates their exultation together with their determination to accomplish their end. On two former occasions they applied for, and obtained from their friends all over the country £o0,00() and £ 1 00,000 þÿ now they demand £250,000 and no one who knows anything of the fixedness of their purpose, aud

Frowt Weekly Messenger, London , October 20, 1 845. ERUPTION OF MOUNT HEOLA. The Borsen Halle contains the following communication from Copenhagen, under date of October 4 t þÿ "The English journals have already stated that the largest of the Orkney isles was, during a violent storm from the north west on the night of the 2d ult , covered with fine ashes resembling ground pumicestone : and that it was thought they had been driven by the wind from Mount Heela, in Iceland, as similar appearances had been observed during several years. We now learn that on the same or the following night the crew of a vessel, bound to this port from Keikisvik. observed, whilst about 18 English miles from land, volcanic flames on the southern aoast of Iceland. On September 3, two vessels near the Fa we Isles were also covered with ashes. According to letters which have been received here, an earthquake occurred on the previous day in the west, north, and east portions of Iceland. More recent intelligence has arrived from the southern part, and it appears that the eruption was a more violent one than any that had taken place there during the last 60 years. The latest accounts are of Sept. 15. They confirm the intelligence of a volcanic eruption in the southern part of the island on Sept. 2, the first since the memorable one which occurted 19 years ago. The extent of the fall of sand and ashes is not yet known, but it is ascertained that the populous districts adjacent to the volcano have not been seriously injured, except that the grass plots near the mountains were destroyed '

The Kj obenhuvnspost, a Danish journal, gives the following account of the new eruption of Mount llecla : þÿ "Hecla, after reposing 80 years, threatens, according to private letters, to ravage Iceland. In the night of he 1st of September a frightful subterranean groaning filled the inhabitants around it with terror. This continued till mid day on the 2d, when the mountain hurst in two places with a horrible crash, and vomited masses of hie. In former times these explosions came from the summit, where Hecla has no regularly formed crater ; hut this time torrents of lava flowed down two gorges on the flanks of the mountain þÿ Letters from Reikjavik of the 13'h state that op to that day no great damage had been done in the Syssels of Rangervalla and Arnds, situated close to the mountain, inasmuch as the openings whence the ignited masses issue are fortunately on the north and north-west sides, and, consequently, took that direction, in which there is nothing hut barren heaths. Besides, the wind having constantly blown lrom the south and south-west, has driven the ashes and dust towards the opposite points. From the clouds of smoke and vapour the top of the volcano could not be seen. The sheep on the heaths were driven down to the plains, but not till several of them were burnt. The waters of the neighbouring rivers near the eruption became so hot that the fish were killed, and it was impossible for any one to ford them even on horseback. Although the lava and ashes took a northern direction, the

caption was not known on licit side of the island till after the 1 1th, and even as lute as the I5tii the people at t h« Svssels ol Muie. in the north cast, were ignorant of it In the western parts, the noise accompanying the eruption was distinctly heard, like the rolling ol distant thunder."

From Peru þÿ The N. O. Picayune learns from Mr. Uryant, who arrived at New Orleans on the 25lh, the following items of news. Mr. II. left Lima on the 7th Sept, taking passage at Callao for Panama on the same day. þÿ All then was quiet at Lima. The Peruvian Congress was still in session there. That body has recently had op for discussion the subject of American claims. The Con-

gress confirmed the convention concluded in 1844, liquidating these claims, but, allowing interest to the claimants only from and alter Jan. 181(1. Gen. Castella makes a popular President, and present appearances would seem to indicate that several years of peace and tranquility may now reign in that hitherto distracted country, and vet, such is the spirit of popular discontent auu rivalry among its numerous aspirants to popular favor there, that many of the most intelligent of the people anticipate another revolution, to follow soon alter the breaking up of Congress. Eqnador on the North, is just out of a similar conflict, Flores is banished, and the Congress of the Republic is about to convene to elect a new President, Gen. Stagg an English officer, who fought in all the wars of the Republic, and who married the daughter of the late President Flores, temporarily left the country as Charge þÿd Affaires to Peru, just before the retirement of his father in law. He ctime to Lima, and after remaining short two months, (his family then at Quito,) he left on his return home. There was a certain widow residing in Brooklyn, i8.'f þÿ , who had a son that was a sailor, þÿ a wild spendthrift of a fellow, merry and thoughtless from natural inclination, and estranged from parental guidance by his roving course of life. His father having been a seafaring man for many years, had saved sufficient money to enable himself and wife to live independent ; at his death, which took place when their child was some seven vears old. the widow removed the boy from school, so that he grew up in ignorance and vicious habits. Living near the river, without manv campatiions about him, his mind naturally imbibed a love for aquatic sports, and he became early versed in naval science, which so grew upon him that at Ins twelfth year he entered the U. S. Navy, where he remained for three years and deserted From this time he embarked in the merchant service, in which he continued to remain, but seldom failing to visit his mother when on shore, who supplied him with money whenever he. needed it. At the time here spoken of, he became less fieqnent in his visits to the parental house, owing to his þÿmother solicitude s for him to abjure his reckless and dissipated vagaries. However, with a view to obviate this difficulty, the widow made her property over to a Mr Chappel, who was to act as her agent, giving him lull power to advance any sums which her son might require through necessity, and to receive anv rent that was forthcoming. The estate consisted of several houses and a con-
iderahle tract of land, and had been valued

The widow herself lived in an obscure and gloomy apartment, at the rear of a narrow and unfrequented sirt-ei, where the bright sunshine seldom entered, and the voice of merriment never was heard: it seemed tar more like a dungeon than the habitation of bereaved humanity. Truly, if melancholy ever had a home, it was in this sequesteied spot, where dreariness and daikness had blended in one universal gloom. MM Novel þÿI mi m. no Mi:chine.--A punting machine ol a novel const ruction has latelv been invented by Mr George Schneldv, an engineer, it is called the Victoria Platten Printing Machine. The noveliv of ihe invention consists in having hut one large wheel and two cog wheels, one larger than the other. In the larger of these there is an eccentric groove, in which two shafts work, one each side : the larger of the shafts forces up the platen, and the smaller carries the paper under the platen, and discharges and adjusts it. When the larger of these shahs is moving the smaller one stops, and when the larger one is moving the smaller one stops, and when the smaller <>ne is moving the larger stops, and wee ueisa. There is another contrivance attached to the smaller shall, hy which the type is better and more equally inked. It is capable at pit-sent of punting between six and eight bundled impressions an hour; a contrivance which though not calculated to compete with steam printing presses, may he found useful in small establishments, it being a great improvement on the old press.

Choctaw þÿCoi'ktsiiip Privileges of the SyuAWs þÿ Courtship invariably begun is by the female. If she fancies a young man, she makes what is technically called the fust banter. This is done by slightly squeezing the hand, or gently touching his foot at t lie camp fire. If a man should venture upon any of the little preliminaries, without being sure of a reciprocal partiality, the indignant maid would immediately assail him with a stick, and this would he the signal for a general assault by all the squaws around on the presuming lover, who. unless he fled, would he beaten without mercy. Thus, even in this rude shape, does women play the coquette ! The young squaw who screams loudest and shows the most resentment to these tin warrantable liberties of an anient luver, is set down as the Diana of her ttibc.

Giving the first banter seems to he reserved by the women as a special prerogative, and they seldom allow it to he infringed with impunity þÿ never in the presence ol a tfiird person. This extends even to their dances, for the squaw always selects her partu , and sends the master of the ceremonies alter him, and he is not permitted to refuse. It is at these dances that elopements ol mat t ied women with young wartiors generally take place. The woman slips out ol the dance at a moment when the confusion is greatest, and repairs to a point agreed upon where she is soon followed by her lover. They usually remain in the woods three or four davs. and when they return live as man and wife, without being molested. Hence elopements are common. The squaws have another privilege which they often exercise. When one chooses a partner for the dance to whom another is attached, her rival closely watches them, and at the first favourable opportunity cuts in, or in other words cuts out the other, leaping into her place with the agility of a fawn, and the mortified dunseuse must silently retire from the circle. Old widows, we have ascertained, Ire. quently give the banters before described, and in many cases they tnatry young fellows under twenty-one. A squaw ol a certain age, if she has seen thirty, is generally provided with a house and some other appliances, and it is considered quite a speculation for a voting man to be supported by one of them lor a year or two At the expiration
of that period, they are generally abandoned for a young wile.

An Eccentihc. þÿ In noticing the death, in Delaware Township, New Jersey, of Mr, Richard Bickford Hodge, the Comden Mail states some curious particulars in relation to the deceased, lie was about 35 years of age, was nit Englishman by birth, had recent- Iv bought a farm, and was evidently a inan of education, who had mingled with good society. He had n<> family, lived entirely alone, with the exception of his dog, and shunned ail intercourse with those near him. 4/u Friday wok he was taken sick, and to the oiler of a neighbour to minister to his wants he returned a decided negative. He peiemptorily rejected all proflered aid, and insisted upon paying for any and every act of kindness. During Friday he set out to reach his next þÿneighbour house, s with a note which he wished conveyed to a tanner a mile or two distant, with whom he had been much less reserved. This farmer came to his assistance, and-called in Dr. Cooper on Sunday. The doctor found Mr. Hodge in the cellar of his house, upon some straw, labouring under much mental excitement, and a monomania that he was pursued by individuals from England, who were at toe time infusing deadly gases into the surrounding atmosphere with intent to destroy him. In other respects he appeared to be sane, conversing with the doctor in a connected and intelligible manner. The doctor did not think him in imminent danger, although quite a sick man, and left him, intending to call next day. In the evening, about seven o'clock, he died, the friend he had sent for,
and his wife, being alone oresent. 1 fie coroner took possession o! I s property, which consisted of a collection ot choice aud valua-

ble book, an extensive and elegant wardrobe, a oonsiderabie sum of ready money, together wiih vaiious articles of ornament and personal comtort, indicative of a decree of intelligence and refinement totally at variance with his late coarse and anchorislic habits of life. His house was destitute of a bed, bedstead, and almost every other article of commonest necessity ! His farm, on which he had lived since March, is bearing a luxuriant crop of weeds. He had neither horse nor cow, spade nor hoe, and refused all applications either (or its cultivation or improvement- He stated before his decease that he had neither relative nor friend in this country. He came originally from Devonshire, and has a brother and two sisters in England. þÿ Philadelphia Inquirer.
